why: A forecast that looks great on shuffled data can fail badly in production. Backtesting is how you prove a forecast works before it drives inventory or staffing.
explain: **Never shuffle time.** You cannot use tomorrow's newspaper to predict today. Train on the past, test on the future.
**Rolling-origin backtest**: train up to month 24, forecast months 25–27; then train up to 27, forecast 28–30; and so on. Average the errors across windows.
Watch out for **look-ahead leakage** in features: rolling means must only use past values, and external data must be "as known at the time".
Metrics: MAE and RMSE in units; **MAPE** or **WAPE** for percentages; **MASE** compares against a naive forecast. **Always compare against a naive baseline** (last value, or same period last year).

example.title: WAPE versus MAPE on four products
steps: One week, four SKUs. Actuals: 100, 80, 120, 10. Forecasts: 90, 88, 108, 20
example.result: MAPE says 32.5% because one tiny SKU missed by 10 units; WAPE's 12.9% reflects the business impact far better. Choose the metric before looking at the results, then score it in a rolling-origin backtest against a naive baseline.

mistakes: Features computed with future data (centred rolling windows).
Reporting a single lucky test window.
takeaways: Train on the past, test on the future, roll forward

practice.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
actual, fcst = np.array([100, 80, 120, 10]), np.array([90, 88, 108, 20])
err = np.abs(actual - fcst)
print("MAPE", (err / actual).mean().round(3), "WAPE", (err.sum() / actual.sum()).round(3))   # 0.325 0.129
y = np.arange(36)
for tr, te in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=4, test_size=3).split(y):
    print("train up to", tr[-1], "→ test", te)

formula.plain: Weighted absolute percentage error: total absolute miss divided by total actual volume, so big sellers count more and tiny items cannot blow it up.
